arguments.name: Boat Owner vs Safety-Conscious Consumer Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Recruit two groups: (1) private boat owners (n=200) and (2) safety-conscious consumers (n=200). Each group views a product description of an ACR marine safety beacon priced at $700. Boat owners receive a marine safety scenario; safety-conscious consumers receive a general safety scenario. Both groups indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1-7).
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 boat owners, 200 safety-conscious consumers) from the US, recruited via marine and outdoor safety forums.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score for each group on the 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Boat owners will show higher purchase intent than safety-conscious consumers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Safety-conscious consumers will show higher purchase intent than boat owners.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for boat owners is at least 1.5 points higher than for safety-conscious consumers, proceed to develop a marine safety proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not commit to a consumer proposition and conduct further research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's technology is approved for general public use and is already sold to commercial marine users, but it does not demonstrate that private boat owners will purchase a marine safety beacon or that they are willing to pay a premium price. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to measure demand before investing.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Deere had a prototype lawn tractor built in 1959 and was evaluating competitive models, but it does not demonstrate household demand for a branded, differentiated unit or that Deere can capture value at a premium. Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to validate purchase intent and reason before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-1962
No access to internal company data or financial figures
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeframe for any proposed experiment
Must consider the existing distribution network of independent dealers and the current reach to individual buyers
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening, or light construction)

Maintain the current business model with no expansion (continue selling through independent dealers)
Target a different customer group (e.g., small farms, hobby farmers, or urban property owners) rather than a specific use case

T1.claim: Households will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a versatile tool for small-scale tasks, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit at a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing household garden size and interest in DIY in the 1960s make a dedicated lawn tractor attractive; the tractor's versatility and Deere's brand signal quality justify a premium purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells a branded, differentiated unit through independent dealers at a higher price point than generic tractors, earning margin on the product.
assumptions: Households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to buy a dedicated lawn tractor.
Deere's engineering reputation translates into consumer trust.
Independent dealers can effectively promote and sell a differentiated product.
predictions: In a test offering a branded lawn tractor at a 20% premium over a generic equivalent, purchase intent among target homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a generic tractor.
Sales conversion rate will be at least 5% among households shown the branded unit.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and purchase intent questions.
X1.sample: 300 U.S. homeowners aged 30-65 who have a small garden or yard, recruited via a panel. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a branded, differentiated lawn tractor at a 20% premium over a generic equivalent; Condition B receives a generic lawn tractor at the same price. Both conditions present the same product description and price.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: "Would you purchase this product?" and a 7-point Likert scale for willingness to pay. Secondary measure: stated reason for purchase (e.g., versatility, specific task, reliability).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Condition B, and the primary reason will be versatility.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Condition A, and the primary reason will be a specific task (e.g., mowing).

X1.decision_rule: If Condition A purchase intent >= 15% AND reason is versatility, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If Condition B purchase intent >= 15% AND reason is a specific task, develop a specialized line. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Deere had a prototype lawn tractor built in 1959 and was evaluating competitive models, but it does not demonstrate household demand for a branded, differentiated unit or that Deere can capture value at a premium. Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to validate purchase intent and reason before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
final.value_proposition: A branded, differentiated lawn tractor that offers versatility and reliability, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (Condition A vs. Condition B) to measure purchase intent and reason for purchase.
final.uncertainty: The size of the household market for lawn tractors in 1962 and whether Deere can capture value at a premium are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows Condition A purchase intent >= 15% and the primary reason is versatility, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.
If the test shows Condition B purchase intent >= 15% and the primary reason is a specific task, we would develop a specialized line of lawn tractors.
If neither condition meets its threshold, we would maintain the current business model with no expansion.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a differentiated garden tractor. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a description emphasizing practicality, affordability, and versatility for small-scale tasks; Group B sees a description emphasizing status, branding, and convenience as a modern ownership symbol. Both groups are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium.
X1.sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and garden ownership, stratified to ensure representation across regions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of status vs practicality.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in Group A exceeds Group B by at least 15% (e.g., €800 vs €700), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on practicality. If Group B exceeds Group A by at least 15%, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced status-focused proposition. If the difference is <15%, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address household purchase motivations or demand for a differentiated garden tractor. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network to sell a branded, practical garden tractor at a premium price.
final.target_customer: Households with small gardens seeking convenient, affordable landscaping solutions
final.value_proposition: A differentiated garden tractor that combines Deere's engineering reputation with a consumer-friendly design, sold through independent dealers to offer convenience and brand trust.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 households, two randomized exposure groups, willingness-to-pay threshold of 15% premium) to validate demand for a practical proposition.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition are unknown; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B (status-focused) exceeding Group A by at least 15% in purchase intent and willingness to pay, we would shift to a premium-priced status proposition.
If no test result meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated offering.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a description emphasizing practicality, affordability, and versatility for small-scale tasks; Group B sees a description emphasizing status, branding, and convenience as a modern ownership symbol. Both groups are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium.
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and garden ownership, stratified to ensure representation across regions.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of status vs practicality.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in Group A exceeds Group B by at least 15% (e.g., €800 vs €700), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on practicality. If Group B exceeds Group A by at least 15%, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced status-focused proposition. If the difference is <15%, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network to sell a branded, practical garden tractor at a premium price. The evidence shows growing household garden size and the tractor's affordability and versatility, supporting the practical demand hypothesis.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network to sell a branded, practical garden tractor at a premium price.
arguments.target_customer: Households with small gardens seeking convenient, affordable landscaping solutions
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated garden tractor that combines Deere's engineering reputation with a consumer-friendly design, sold through independent dealers to offer convenience and brand trust.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 households, two randomized exposure groups, willingness-to-pay threshold of 15% premium) to validate demand for a practical proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition are unknown; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B (status-focused) exceeding Group A by at least 15% in purchase intent and willingness to pay, we would shift to a premium-priced status proposition.
If no test result meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated offering.

X1.name: Branded vs. Generic Lawn Tractor Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 homeowners in the United States who have small garden areas (e.g., 1,000 sq ft). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A sees a branded Deere lawn tractor described as versatile for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup, priced at 20% above a generic equivalent. Group B sees the same generic tractor at the same price. Both groups are shown a brief description of the product and a call-to-action to purchase. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this lawn tractor?") and willingness to pay (maximum price).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners with small garden areas, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (maximum price) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, because the branded unit is positioned as versatile and justified by the 1962 lawn equipment sales surge.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group A, because the specialized unit is positioned for a specific recurring task and is justified by the demand for a dedicated mower.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the branded unit (Group A) is at least 15% higher than for the generic unit (Group B), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (supporting T1). If purchase intent for the generic unit (Group B) is at least 15% higher, maintain the current model without expansion (supporting T2). If neither difference meets the 15% threshold, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment.

arguments.name: Branded vs. Generic Lawn Tractor Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 homeowners in the United States who have small garden areas (e.g., 1,000 sq ft). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A sees a branded Deere lawn tractor described as versatile for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup, priced at 20% above a generic equivalent. Group B sees the same generic tractor at the same price. Both groups are shown a brief description of the product and a call-to-action to purchase. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this lawn tractor?") and willingness to pay (maximum price).
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners with small garden areas, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two groups.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (maximum price) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, because the branded unit is positioned as versatile and justified by the 1962 lawn equipment sales surge.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group A, because the specialized unit is positioned for a specific recurring task and is justified by the demand for a dedicated mower.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the branded unit (Group A) is at least 15% higher than for the generic unit (Group B), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (supporting T1). If purchase intent for the generic unit (Group B) is at least 15% higher, maintain the current model without expansion (supporting T2). If neither difference meets the 15% threshold, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Deere had a prototype lawn tractor built in 1959 and began production in 1963, but it does not demonstrate household demand for a branded, differentiated unit or that Deere can capture value at a premium. The 1962 lawn equipment sales surge supports the idea that demand exists, but it does not address whether a differentiated use‑
